claim: Treat presentation of a UI as a required deliverable, not an optional garnish: budget explicit time for composing the screens after the interface itself is done.
why: The narration asserts the raw artboard is only half the work — a design's reception depends on the frame it arrives in, so shipping unpresented screens leaves half the value on the table.
when: Any time a UI leaves your hands for someone else's eyes — client review, portfolio, case study, social post, pitch deck.
fails: Not addressed in the intro; presumably irrelevant for internal working files, dev handoff specs, or engineering-facing artifacts where legibility beats staging.

claim: Choose the presentation treatment to match the audience and context rather than applying one house style — a creative/portfolio audience and a professional/client audience warrant different compositions of the same screens.
why: The chapter promises to show one design presented multiple ways specifically split by creative versus professional settings, implying the correct treatment is context-dependent, not absolute.
when: Deciding how to stage a finished UI when the same work will be shown to different audiences.
fails: Not addressed in this chapter.

claim: Keep presentation treatment independent of the design's own aesthetic register — a restrained interface and an expressive one both benefit from deliberate staging, so don't skip presentation because the work is 'simple'.
why: The narration lists opposed registers (simple/stunning, imaginative/professional) and claims presentation improves all of them, implying staging is an orthogonal layer rather than something reserved for showy work.
when: Presenting minimal, utilitarian, or enterprise UI that seems to need no dressing.
fails: Not addressed; presentation that overwhelms a deliberately quiet design would presumably work against it.

claim: Derive showcase background colours from the design's own accent colour rather than picking an unrelated colour: take the accent, darken it, and desaturate it toward grey.
why: A background sampled from the palette stays harmonious, while desaturating and darkening ensures it recedes; a background at full chroma competes with the UI for attention and wins.
when: Light-mode showcase shots on a plain background, where you need a colour that relates to the design without upstaging it.
fails: When the design has no distinct accent, or when the piece is intentionally about the background (brand-identity work), a derived neutral may be too timid.

claim: On a plain background, add a faint drop shadow under the UI frame — low opacity, generous blur — rather than letting the frame sit flush against the colour.
why: A soft shadow separates the artboard from the backdrop and reads as depth without adding any visual noise.
when: Minimal single-frame showcases on a solid background.

claim: For dark-mode showcases, place two or three large heavily blurred circles of the accent colour behind the UI instead of using a shadow.
why: On a dark field a shadow is invisible; blurred accent blobs read as ambient light bouncing off the screen, making the UI look self-illuminating.
when: Dark backgrounds, especially for products with a saturated brand colour and glowing UI elements.
fails: Light-mode compositions, where a glow reads as haze or a rendering artifact rather than emitted light.

claim: When placing UI on a translucent glass panel, define its edges with a soft gradient stroke rather than a uniform 1px line.
why: A gradient stroke mimics how light catches an edge unevenly, which sells the material and adds a depth layer the flat fill cannot.
when: Glassmorphic or layered showcase backgrounds.

claim: Default to the minimal treatment — flat background, faint shadow — unless you have a specific reason to escalate.
why: Bland backgrounds are the most reliable way to make the design itself the loudest object in the frame, and the technique is near-impossible to execute badly across design types.
when: Any showcase where the UI is the subject and you are unsure which treatment fits.
fails: Feeds where every competing post is minimal, or briefs that explicitly reward visual invention.

claim: 'Explode' the composition by letting one element — a chart line, a background pattern, a slider track — extend past the frame edge instead of cropping it cleanly at the boundary.
why: A bleeding element implies the design continues beyond the canvas, which is more visually interesting than a contained rectangle; the same content cropped tight reads as flat.
when: Single-frame hero shots that feel static and need motion without changing the UI itself.
fails: Presentations meant to communicate the actual product, since the exploded version misrepresents the real layout and is 'not super practical'.

claim: The exploding element does not have to come from the UI — pull a shape from the brand's visual identity and attach real metrics to it.
why: Extending the identity rather than the interface keeps the composition on-brand while giving you a graphic element with far more freedom than a screenshot region.
when: Brand-adjacent product work where the visual identity is strong enough to carry a composition.

claim: When skewing a UI frame, keep the transform small — on the order of a couple of degrees on one axis and roughly ten to fifteen on the other (e.g. 2° vertical, -14° horizontal).
why: A small skew reads as a deliberate perspective cue that draws the eye; a large one distorts the interface until the content becomes unreadable and the shot stops being about the design.
when: Adding dynamism to a static frame or to a whole multi-screen group.
fails: Text-dense screens where even mild skew degrades legibility, and any context where the viewer must actually read the UI.

claim: To emphasise one element within a skewed composition, offset it from its original position, give it its own shadow, and optionally leave a flat grey placeholder in the slot it vacated.
why: The offset plus shadow lifts the element onto a nearer depth plane, and the ghost placeholder makes the displacement legible as intentional rather than as a misalignment.
when: One region of the screen (a hero card, a key chart) matters more than the rest.
fails: When the placeholder adds clutter — the ghost is optional and should be dropped if the pop-out already reads.

claim: Never present multiple screens as a flat stack; offset them from each other and let the outer ones bleed off the canvas edge.
why: Evenly stacked frames read as an inventory list with no focal point; offsetting creates hierarchy and the bleed implies there is more work than fits.
when: Showing two to four screens of the same product.

claim: In a multi-screen collage, deliberately break grid alignment — stagger the frames rather than snapping them to shared rows and columns.
why: A perfect grid is legible but inert; irregular placement makes the eye travel across the composition.
when: Collages of four or more screens, typically to fill the empty space left by a two-screen offset layout.
fails: Case-study or spec documentation, where a grid's scannability is the point.

claim: Add a few degrees of rotation to a screen group to inject motion, or skew the entire assembled collage as one unit.
why: Rotation and group skew apply the dynamism at the composition level, so individual screens stay internally consistent while the whole reads as in motion.
when: Collage compositions that feel correct but static.

claim: Match the technique to the design's visual scale: use multi-screen collages and skews for coarse designs like landing pages, and avoid them for detail-dense screens.
why: Collage and skew shrink and distort each frame; dashboard-grade detail becomes illegible at that size, so the composition shows texture rather than design.
when: Choosing between single-frame and multi-frame showcase formats.

claim: To showcase a dense interface like a dashboard, crop hard into a single region at high zoom and add a small animation, instead of showing the whole screen small.
why: Zooming trades completeness for legibility — the viewer can actually read one component — and slight motion supplies the interest the collage would have provided.
when: Data-heavy or component-dense products in a feed-scale format.
fails: When the layout itself is the achievement, since a zoomed crop discards it.

claim: Only introduce photography when the image is topically relevant to the product and quiet enough not to compete; otherwise fall back to a background or collage treatment.
why: Images carry more visual weight than any generated background, so the balance between relevance and distraction is the hardest to strike of all the techniques.
when: Products with a physical anchor — a café, a vehicle, a physical good — or portfolio templates where imagery is already part of the UI.
fails: Pure software products, where relevant imagery rarely exists and a fluid gradient render or an earlier technique usually serves better.

claim: Fix the underlying interface before investing in presentation technique.
why: Showcase composition amplifies whatever it frames; a polished frame around weak UI only makes the weakness more visible.
when: Any portfolio piece.

claim: Choose presentation style by audience: for a portfolio use stylized, attention-grabbing compositions; for a client meeting use plain, realistic framing that shows the product as it will actually exist.
why: A portfolio viewer is being persuaded to look; a client is being persuaded to trust. Dramatic staging that wins attention can read as hiding the product from someone who has to approve it.
when: Preparing the same design work for two different venues — a public case study versus a stakeholder review.
fails: The client is themselves buying a visual brand identity or launch campaign, where the aspirational treatment is the deliverable rather than a distraction.

claim: Place every client-facing screen inside a device frame rather than presenting a bare rectangle of UI.
why: The frame supplies scale, platform, and viewing distance, letting the client evaluate the design as a product instead of as an image.
when: Any static screen shown to a non-designer who needs to imagine using the finished thing.
fails: Detailed design critique of spacing, type, or colour, where the frame shrinks the artwork and adds visual noise.

claim: Escalate from an empty device render to a lifestyle shot — hands on the device, a real environment, the interface mid-use — when you want the strongest sense that the product already exists.
why: Showing the interface in the posture and setting where it will actually be used answers the unspoken question of whether it fits into someone's day.
when: Hero shots, project openers, and pitch moments where the point is context of use rather than screen detail.
fails: Environmental clutter, hands, or lighting obscure the interface — the scene must never win over the screen.

claim: Match the mockup device to the current flagship hardware for its platform rather than an older model.
why: Recognisably outdated hardware quietly dates the work and suggests the designer is not current.
when: Selecting or generating any device mockup for client or portfolio use.
fails: The product genuinely targets legacy or low-end devices, or a specific enterprise hardware fleet, where the real device is the honest choice.

claim: Generate custom mockup photography with an image model, but keep the interface itself hand-designed.
why: Generative models produce convincing photographic surfaces, materials, and lighting, but not the hierarchy and logic an interface needs — so use them for the container, not the contents.
when: You need staging that free mockup packs cannot provide and cannot justify a photo shoot.
fails: Treating the model's output as a design source — asking it to lay out the screen rather than the scene around it.

claim: Write mockup prompts as a stacked list of specifics: device, a flat green fill on the screen, the supporting surface and its material, one or two background props, the depth-of-field treatment, shadow softness, and a lighting mood.
why: Each named attribute removes a decision the model would otherwise make generically; roughly two or three dozen words of specifics is enough to get a usable, non-stock-looking frame.
when: Generating any device or product mockup image.
fails: Piling on so many competing details that the model loses the device geometry or renders a screen that cannot be cleanly keyed out.

claim: Ask for a solid green screen fill on the device display so you can key it out and perspective-warp your real screenshot into the exact quad.
why: A uniform, saturated fill gives a clean selection edge and an unambiguous four-corner target for the distort, keeping the pipeline to a couple of minutes.
when: Compositing a designed screen into any AI-generated or photographed device.
fails: The scene reflects green onto surrounding surfaces, or the design contains greens that get caught by the key.

claim: Specify the incidental imperfections — a hairline crack, a water stain, a worn surface, a lived-in room — instead of asking for a pristine scene.
why: Flawlessness reads as rendered; small irregularities are what make a viewer accept the image as a photograph, which is exactly the credibility the mockup is there to borrow.
when: Generating environments, props, and product shots meant to pass as real photography.
fails: Damage suggestions attach to the product itself in a commercial context, implying the item you are selling is defective.

claim: Apply the same generated-mockup method to product and packaging shots for e-commerce work, not just device screens.
why: In commerce the photograph carries most of the purchase decision, so mockup quality is a direct commercial variable rather than a presentation nicety.
when: Designing storefronts, product pages, or brand systems where you control the imagery.

claim: Whenever a behaviour is easier to demonstrate than to describe, ship a clickable prototype instead of writing a caption.
why: A static frame plus explanation asks the viewer to simulate the interaction mentally; a prototype lets them see it and then feel it, which is far more convincing.
when: Presenting flows, transitions, or anything with a time dimension.

claim: Prototype specifically the affordances that are invisible at rest — swipe actions, long-press menus, and other gestures hidden behind a static state.
why: These interactions are intuitive to use but impossible to see in a screenshot, so a still image silently understates the product's capability.
when: Mobile patterns and any interface where functionality is revealed by gesture.

claim: Record the entry and exit choreography of overlays and destructive actions — how a creation modal animates in, what sequence plays when an item is deleted.
why: Transition craft is the clearest available evidence of thoroughness; it signals that the work extends past the states someone remembered to draw.
when: Dashboards, CRUD-heavy tools, and other product surfaces judged on feel rather than novelty.

claim: Build 3D web assets from a vector source: draw the shape as an SVG in your 2D design tool, import it into the 3D app, and extrude it into geometry rather than modelling from scratch.
why: The vector path already carries the exact silhouette from the design system, so extrusion transfers brand-accurate shapes into 3D with no modelling skill and no drift between the 2D and 3D versions of the mark.
when: Producing 3D logos, icons, or badges that must match an existing flat design.
fails: Organic, non-extrudable forms or anything needing real volume and topology — a flat profile pushed along one axis reads as a cookie cutter.

claim: Treat the 3D asset pipeline as a fixed five-step sequence — import vector, extrude, place camera, light the scene, apply materials — and only then export.
why: The steps are dependency-ordered: geometry must exist before framing, framing before lighting, lighting before material judgement, since a material only reads correctly under the lights and angle it will ship with.
when: Any first pass at a 3D hero element, in any 3D tool.

claim: Pick the 3D tool by which stage of the project you are in: use the lightweight browser-based tool (Spline) for fast iteration and animation you need to preview immediately, and the heavyweight tool (Blender) when material quality is the deciding factor.
why: The lighter tool's value is round-trip speed and an in-app animation preview that shows the real result; the heavier tool's value is a shading system that produces convincing metallic and reflective surfaces, paid for in learning time.
when: Choosing between 3D tools for a single hero asset on a deadline.
fails: When the asset must be interactive in the browser — the render-quality advantage is irrelevant if the output has to ship as a live scene rather than a baked render.

claim: Budget the learning curve as a real line item: expect the higher-quality tool to cost several hours of tutorial-following before the first usable output.
why: The quality gap between tools is not free, and planning as if both take the same time causes the better-looking option to get cut late in the project.
when: Scoping a project that includes a technique you have not used before.

claim: It is acceptable to reproduce a material setup from a tutorial without understanding the underlying node graph, provided you judge the result visually.
why: Shading systems are deep enough that comprehension is a poor gate on shipping; the render is the only thing the audience sees, so visual evaluation is the actual acceptance test.
when: One-off hero assets where a specific surface look is the goal, not building reusable shading skill.
fails: When the material must be varied, re-lit, or reused across many assets — a copied graph you cannot read is not adjustable.

claim: Make material treatment the differentiator on a 3D hero asset, not the geometry — a simple extruded shape with a convincing metallic surface outperforms complex geometry with flat shading.
why: The extruded silhouette is identical between both attempts here, so the entire perceived quality difference traces to the shading and reflections.
when: Logo and icon work where the form is fixed by brand.

claim: Verify the animation inside the 3D tool before exporting, and treat 'plays exactly as intended in preview' as the gate for moving to layout.
why: Catching timing or motion-path errors in the authoring environment is far cheaper than discovering them after export and integration into the page.
when: Any animated 3D asset destined for a web build.

claim: When two approaches are viable, build the asset in both and compare finished renders side by side rather than choosing on reputation.
why: Effort and output quality can only be compared honestly once both artefacts exist under the same brief.
when: Early in a project when tooling is undecided and the asset is small enough to duplicate.
fails: Large or complex assets, where duplicating the whole build is a poor use of the schedule.

claim: QA a looping 3D animation across its entire cycle, not at a single pose — step through the full rotation and fix any frames where the surface falls into unlit shadow.
why: A lighting rig tuned to one flattering angle leaves dead zones that only appear mid-rotation, so the asset reads as broken exactly when the user is watching it move.
when: Any continuously animating 3D element on a page — rotating logos, orbiting products, auto-spinning hero objects.
fails: When the darkness is intentional dramatic falloff, or when the object only ever animates through a narrow, art-directed angle range that you can light specifically.

claim: Fix rotation shadowing by adding fill or rim lights around the object rather than by raising the intensity of the existing key light.
why: Boosting the key only blows out the faces already lit; the dark spots are unlit angles, which need light sources positioned to cover them.
when: Debugging uneven illumination on a spinning object in a 3D scene.
fails: Highly reflective or glass-like materials, where the visual problem is usually the environment/HDRI map rather than discrete lights.

claim: Budget roughly two hours of modelling and lighting per hero-scale 3D asset when you are new to the tool, and scope the page to the number of assets that budget allows.
why: Concrete per-asset timing lets you quote and schedule 3D work instead of treating it as an open-ended experiment.
when: Estimating a landing page that features custom 3D objects rather than stock or purchased models.
fails: Assets needing rigging, character work, complex simulation, or photoreal material studies — those run far beyond a couple of hours.

claim: Ship a 3D scene with a known minor flaw rather than delaying the build, but write the flaw down explicitly as a revision item.
why: Naming the defect out loud keeps the shortcut deliberate and traceable instead of letting it pass as an accepted result.
when: Time-boxed builds, demos, and first-pass client presentations.
fails: Final client delivery or brand-critical marketing pages, where a visibly broken logo animation undermines the whole piece.

claim: Give each 3D asset its own full-height scroll section with room around it instead of stacking several into one dense viewport.
why: A 3D object needs the full frame to be legible as a form — separate sections let each one register at scale as the user scrolls.
when: Marketing or portfolio pages where the 3D asset is the primary visual, not a decorative accent.
fails: Content-heavy pages where repeated full-height scroll sections push actual information below several screens of decoration.

claim: Treat basic 3D asset production as a billable service extension: learn it in short sessions and offer it as an option clients cannot get from a generic template.
why: The barrier is a handful of hours, not a career change, so the differentiation-to-effort ratio is unusually favourable for a designer already doing web work.
when: Freelance or studio designers looking to widen what they can quote for.
fails: Projects with performance-constrained audiences or accessibility-first requirements, where heavy 3D is the wrong recommendation regardless of skill.

claim: When a project needs product imagery you can't photograph or render well, buy or download a mockup template that already matches the product form, and spend your effort on the artwork placed inside it rather than on the render.
why: Your output quality should be capped by your strongest skill, not your weakest; a stock mockup buys photographic realism for free so the design work stays on the surface that actually communicates the brand.
when: Presenting physical products, packaging, or devices in a UI/marketing comp where you lack photography or 3D skills.
fails: The product form is unusual enough that no template matches it, or the mockup's lighting and style clash with the rest of the design system — a mismatched mockup reads cheaper than no image.

claim: Before producing marketing or hero imagery, audit the source design for brand assets it silently lacks — logo, wordmark, name — and create the missing ones first, because downstream artwork can't be finished without them.
why: Packaging, mockups, and headers all consume the identity; discovering it's absent mid-render forces rework.
when: Redesigning an existing site or app that has to be extended into product shots, packaging, or any off-screen surface.

claim: Choose a brand name that carries the category's existing associations rather than one that is merely clever — for beauty and skincare, a short elegant personal name in a language the market codes as luxurious does most of the positioning work before any type is set.
why: A name is the cheapest positioning signal you have; borrowing an association the audience already holds means the visual design doesn't have to fight to establish tone.
when: Inventing a placeholder or real brand for a concept project in a category with strong naming conventions.
fails: Borrowing cultural cues you don't understand can produce names that are nonsense or offensive to native speakers — verify a plausible name with someone who speaks the language.

claim: Study real products in the category before designing packaging, but treat the reference as data about conventions, not as a style target to copy.
why: Mass-market packaging is optimised for shelf competition and regulatory copy, so it's dense by necessity; that density is the opposite of the restraint a premium positioning needs.
when: Designing packaging, labels, or any physical artefact for a category you haven't worked in.
fails: If the brand actually competes on shelf rather than online, stripping the informational density can make the product illegible to shoppers.

claim: To read as premium and minimal, cut the number of distinct elements on the pack to the minimum: brand mark, product name, one descriptor, volume — and delete decorative badges, secondary claims, and ornament.
why: Perceived luxury correlates with restraint and empty space; every added element lowers the apparent value of the ones already there.
when: Packaging or label design for a brand positioned as high-end or minimal.
fails: Value or mass-market brands, where communicating benefits and claims outranks aesthetic restraint.

claim: Don't centre two stacked elements on the same vertical axis when they have different widths or weights — pick one to hold the centre and shift the other to an edge so the axis reads as deliberate rather than as a failed alignment.
why: Two centred items of unequal width create a wobbling, ambiguous axis; a clear contrast between a centred anchor and an edge-aligned secondary element reads as an intentional composition.
when: Laying out a small surface such as a label, card, or pack face with a dominant mark and one or more supporting text blocks.
fails: In a strictly symmetrical layout where every element shares a width, centring everything is the stronger, calmer choice.

claim: Pair hand-drawn marks with a rigid, high-contrast typeface (heavy weight, tight cut) rather than with another informal or script face — the effect comes from the collision of precise and imprecise, not from a uniformly casual page.
why: The visual interest is generated by contrast between the two registers; if both layers are loose, there is nothing for the scribble to read against and the page just looks unresolved.
when: Building a landing page, hero section, or promo block where you want personality without commissioning illustration.
fails: The whole design is already informal, script-based, or texture-heavy — adding hand-drawn marks there produces mush instead of contrast.

claim: Use hand-drawn marks as annotation on top of existing type — circle a key word, underline a phrase, point an arrow at the CTA — rather than as standalone decorative illustration floating in empty space.
why: Annotation marks inherit meaning from the text they touch, so they double as emphasis and hierarchy rather than being pure ornament that the eye can skip.
when: You want to direct attention to one word or one action in a text-dominant layout.
fails: There is no clear single element worth emphasising — circling several things at once flattens the emphasis back to zero.

claim: Soften hand-drawn layers slightly — a small blur, reduced opacity, or a softer stroke — so they sit visually behind the crisp type instead of competing with it for the first read.
why: It establishes z-order and reading order optically: the sharp layer reads first as content, the softer layer reads second as commentary.
when: Overlaying handwriting or scribble on top of headline typography.
fails: The mark is the primary content (e.g. a hand-lettered logo), where softening just makes it look like a rendering error.

claim: When a page's visual weight is carried by hand-drawn marks, keep the copy deliberately sparse — a headline and a short line beneath it — instead of filling the space with body text.
why: The drawn elements need negative space around them to read as intentional gesture; dense copy turns them into clutter competing for the same area.
when: Hero sections and single-purpose landing pages using the illustrated/annotated style.
fails: Content-heavy pages such as docs, dashboards, or long-form marketing where the copy is the product.

claim: Attach a hover state to hand-drawn elements — animating the stroke, swapping the mark, or nudging the drawing — so the informality extends into the interaction rather than stopping at the static composition.
why: A drawn line implies it was made by a hand in time; animating it on interaction pays off that implication and makes the style feel authored rather than stock.
when: Product cards, nav links, or CTAs on a site already committed to the hand-drawn aesthetic.

claim: Draw the marks yourself with a vector pencil/brush tool at the size they will be displayed, keeping stroke weight consistent across every mark on the page.
why: A consistent stroke reads as one hand and one pen; mismatched weights read as clip-art assembled from different sources.
when: Producing the asset set — circles, underlines, arrows, asterisks — for a hand-drawn system.

claim: Budget real time for this style despite how simple it looks; the polish sits in the placement, timing, and stroke quality, not in the act of scribbling.
why: The narrator repeatedly walks back the 'just scribble on it' framing, signalling that the finished examples involve considerably more craft than the shorthand implies.
when: Estimating effort for an annotated or hand-drawn direction.

claim: To build a kaleidoscope surface, stack in this order: radial gradient base, then an angular gradient of alternating black/white segments set to Difference, then a duplicate of that angular layer set to Screen on top of everything.
why: Difference inverts the base colours per wedge to create the mirrored facet structure; Screen on the duplicate lifts the whites back out so the facets read as light rather than muddy inversion.
when: Producing decorative, high-impact surfaces — card faces, sticker art, button fills — in Figma or any tool with layer blend modes.
fails: The Screen copy sits below other layers; anything drawn above it breaks the composite and the effect collapses.

claim: Use an even number of alternating black/white segments in the angular gradient — 6, 8, or 10 are reliable starting points.
why: An even count closes the ring symmetrically so the wedges mirror cleanly around the centre; an odd count leaves two like-coloured segments adjacent at the seam.
when: Generating any radial/angular repeat pattern where the sweep must wrap back to its own start.

claim: When a blend-mode composite depends on a layer, place that layer at the top of the stack and keep it there — treat stacking order as part of the effect's definition, not a cosmetic detail.
why: Blend modes composite against everything rendered beneath them, so inserting a layer above silently changes the maths.
when: Any multi-layer Difference/Screen/Overlay composite.

claim: Add a fine noise/grain layer over flat gradient work to keep it from reading as a sterile digital gradient.
why: Pure vector gradients band and look synthetic; grain reintroduces surface texture and makes the piece feel physical, which matters for objects meant to read as printed or manufactured.
when: Gradient-heavy decorative surfaces, especially ones imitating physical objects like credit cards or stickers.

claim: To integrate type into a chromatic surface rather than sit it on top, use a heavy weight and set the text layer's blend mode to Overlay.
why: Overlay lets the underlying colour drive the letterforms so type reads as part of the material; the extra weight preserves enough mass to survive the reduced contrast.
when: Display or brand type sitting directly on a busy gradient or patterned surface.
fails: Body copy, labels, or anything that must be reliably readable — Overlay makes contrast depend on whatever happens to be behind each letter.

claim: Budget legibility against decoration explicitly, and reserve blend-mode type treatments for surfaces where looking good is the actual job.
why: The chapter concedes the finished piece has poor usability; the treatment is defensible for a sticker or card face and indefensible for an interface control.
when: Choosing where in a product to deploy expressive effects.
fails: Applied to interactive UI — a button built this way may look striking but fails contrast requirements for its label.

claim: Close a dense multi-step visual recipe with a single summary artefact that captures the whole stack at a glance.
why: Procedural layer-and-blend-mode instructions exceed what anyone retains from a linear walkthrough; a reference card converts the demo into something reusable.
when: Documenting or teaching any multi-layer construction technique.

claim: Build a clay surface by stacking two inner shadows on one shape, with offsets pointing in opposite directions, so one darkens the top/right edges and the other darkens the bottom/left edges.
why: A single inner shadow reads as a shape cut into the background; two opposing ones darken the whole rim while leaving the centre bright, which is how a soft rounded solid catches light on all sides.
when: Giving a flat vector shape the look of a soft moldable solid — isometric props, illustration elements, chunky icons.
fails: On thin strokes, small text, or shapes smaller than the shadow blur radius, where the two rims overlap and flatten the whole shape into a muddy blob.

claim: Fill clay-effect shapes with muted, desaturated colours; avoid highly saturated hues.
why: The illusion depends on reading darkened rims as shading of one material; a saturated fill has little headroom to darken and the shadows read as separate grey overlays rather than as the same colour in shade.
when: Any shape receiving the clay treatment, and by extension any effect that simulates shading through darkened variants of the fill.

claim: After the inner shadows, add a soft outer drop shadow to separate the clay object from its background.
why: Inner shadows only model the object's own surface; without a cast shadow the object still sits flush on the canvas instead of resting above it.
when: When the clay object needs to feel like a physical piece placed on a surface rather than a texture painted onto the background.
fails: Optional — omit it when the object is meant to be embedded in or flush with its background.

claim: Prototype a material effect on a plain primitive rectangle before applying it to real artwork.
why: A neutral shape isolates the shadow parameters so you can tune offset, blur, and colour without silhouette complexity confusing the read; the settings then transfer to any shape.
when: Developing or learning a reusable layer-effect recipe.

claim: Keep the two inner shadows as exact mirrors of each other — same blur and spread, inverted X and Y offsets — so no single light direction dominates.
why: Clay reads as diffusely lit; a matched pair produces even rim shading, whereas unequal values reintroduce a directional light and turn the object into a beveled button instead.
when: Configuring the shadow pair for a soft-body material.
fails: When you deliberately want a directional key light — then bias one shadow heavier and lighten the opposite one.

claim: Treat this as a two-inner-shadow template you re-apply across a whole illustration rather than tuning per object.
why: Consistent shadow parameters across elements imply a single material and single lighting environment; per-object variation makes a scene look like assorted objects rather than one clay set.
when: Building an isometric scene or icon set where multiple elements share the clay look.

claim: Build metal surfaces as a stack of layers rather than a single fill: rounded base shape -> multi-stop linear gradient -> overlay-blended white radial highlight -> inner shadows -> optional tint layer.
why: Real metal reads as metal because of layered specular behaviour; no single gradient encodes both the body sheen and the edge thickness, so separating them lets each be tuned independently.
when: Faking a reflective, machined surface in a flat vector tool — credit cards, device chassis, badges, hardware mockups.
fails: The surface is meant to read as matte, plastic, paper, or fabric; the stack will make it look chrome-plated regardless of hue.

claim: In the base linear gradient, place a sharp, high-contrast value jump near the middle of the shape; treat the stops at the two outer edges as low-priority.
why: A metallic read comes from the abrupt light/dark boundary where the surface curvature flips reflection direction — a smooth edge-to-edge ramp reads as plastic or as a plain gradient.
when: Setting up the foundation fill for any brushed or polished metal panel.
fails: If the mid jump is too hard-edged it reads as two separate fills rather than one continuous surface; it needs to be noticeable but still a gradient.

claim: Sample the base gradient from desaturated greys plus dark blues rather than pure neutral greys.
why: Neutral grey reads as dead plastic; cool blue in the shadows simulates the sky/ambient reflection that real polished metal picks up.
when: Choosing the palette for the metal substrate before any tint is applied.

claim: Add depth with a white radial gradient on its own layer set to Overlay blend mode instead of painting a lighter highlight directly into the base gradient.
why: Overlay multiplies the highlight against the underlying values, so the sheen preserves the base gradient's contrast structure and reacts correctly when the base or tint changes.
when: Adding a specular hotspot or a sense of thickness over an existing gradient surface.
fails: Over a base that is already near-white or near-black, Overlay has little value range to act on and the highlight disappears.

claim: Use two stacked inner shadows with different offsets/blurs rather than one, to carve the edge of the shape.
why: One inner shadow gives a single uniform lip; two at different scales separate a tight bevel line from a broader falloff, which is what reads as machined thickness.
when: Giving a flat rounded rectangle the appearance of a physical edge or milled bevel.
fails: At small render sizes the two shadows collapse into a muddy dark rim.

claim: Recolour a finished metal stack by adding a solid colour layer on top at roughly 20% fill opacity, leaving all the underlying layers untouched.
why: A low-opacity tint shifts hue while the greyscale gradient, highlight, and shadows continue to supply the metallic value structure — recolouring the base gradient itself would destroy the contrast that makes it read as metal.
when: Producing colour variants (rose gold, bronze, gold, titanium) from one master metal treatment.
fails: Pushing the tint opacity much higher flattens the value range and the surface stops reading as metal and starts reading as coloured plastic.

claim: Pick tint hues from reds, oranges, and blues to hit recognisable metal finishes — warm reds/oranges for gold, rose gold, and bronze; cool blues for titanium and steel.
why: Named metal finishes are culturally encoded as specific hue families; greens and purples have no metal referent and read as anodised novelty.
when: Choosing the tint colour for a metal variant.

claim: Before investing in a heavy layered surface treatment, check that the subject actually justifies it — reserve full metallic stacks for objects that are physically metal in the mockup.
why: The effect is expensive in layers and visually loud; applied to arbitrary UI surfaces it dominates the composition without earning attention.
when: Deciding whether to reach for this technique at all.

claim: Build a mesh gradient from stacked shapes rather than a single multi-stop gradient fill: one large blurred, low-opacity circle as the base, then additional blurred low-opacity circles layered on top.
why: Overlapping soft blobs produce the irregular, multi-directional colour transitions that a linear or radial gradient cannot, and doing it with native shapes keeps the result editable without plugin dependencies.
when: Creating organic, colourful background fields for hero sections, poster art, or slide backgrounds in a vector tool.
fails: When you need a precise, reproducible gradient token (brand ramps, data-viz scales) or an asset that must stay small and crisp — stacked heavy blurs are expensive to render and hard to spec.

claim: Set the blend mode of every circle above the base layer to Overlay instead of Normal.
why: Normal stacking just paints one colour over another; Overlay makes each layer interact with what is beneath it, so intersections generate new colours rather than occluding.
when: Layering translucent colour blobs where you want the overlaps themselves to be the interesting part of the composition.
fails: Over very light or very dark bases, where Overlay's contrast-dependent maths washes out or crushes the added colour and the layers stop reading.

claim: Treat layer count as the brightness and saturation control: add more overlapping blobs to intensify the gradient, and expect to need roughly 8-10 layers or more for a rich result.
why: Overlay compounds multiplicatively across the stack, so vibrancy accumulates with each intersection rather than arriving from any single layer's colour value.
when: Tuning a mesh that reads flat, muddy, or washed out.
fails: When the composition sits behind text or UI controls — past a certain layer count the field blows out to near-white hotspots and destroys foreground contrast.

claim: Give every circle a blur radius large enough that its edge is no longer perceptible as a circle before you judge the composition.
why: The illusion depends on the viewer seeing colour fields, not shapes; a readable circular edge breaks the mesh into obvious discs.
when: Any stage of building the stack, including the base layer.

claim: Iterate this effect by eye — adjust hue, blur radius, and opacity in a loop and stop when it looks right — rather than deriving values from a formula.
why: The output depends on how the specific colours interact through Overlay, so no fixed parameter set transfers between palettes.
when: Producing a one-off decorative background where the success criterion is aesthetic.
fails: In a design system context where another designer or an engineer must reproduce the exact same surface; there you must capture the result as a flattened asset or documented values.

claim: Reach for the mesh-gradient technique when a surface needs visual interest but no additional content, since the same construction ports across web, print, and presentation formats.
why: It is resolution-independent, built from primitives available in any vector tool, and carries no semantic meaning that would compete with foreground content.
when: Empty or content-light surfaces: hero backgrounds, poster fields, title slides, card backdrops.

claim: For each feature block on a landing page, use a cropped, lightly retouched screenshot of that feature's real UI instead of a generic icon or stock illustration.
why: A real screen proves the feature exists and shows the visitor what they will actually get; a generic icon conveys no product-specific information and reads as filler.
when: Marketing or landing pages for a product whose UI is already designed and presentable — feature grids, benefit sections, hero visuals.
fails: The underlying UI is unfinished or ugly, or the feature is non-visual (compliance, uptime, support) — there the screenshot has nothing to show and an icon or diagram is the honest choice.

claim: Reuse the product screens you already designed as landing-page assets rather than authoring separate marketing artwork.
why: It keeps the marketing page and the product visually consistent, costs no extra design work, and prevents the mismatch where the landing page promises a polish the app doesn't have.
when: Solo builders or small teams shipping product and marketing site together.

claim: Retouch product screenshots before placing them — trim chrome, drop irrelevant regions, and clean up placeholder data — rather than pasting a raw capture.
why: A raw screenshot carries noise (browser chrome, dev data, empty states) that distracts from the one thing the section is selling; a light edit directs attention to the feature being described.
when: Any time real UI is used as a marketing visual.
fails: Editing so heavily that the image no longer reflects the shipped product, which misleads visitors.

claim: Optimise landing pages for presentation quality — visual craft, spacing, imagery — before adding more sections, animations, or copy.
why: Conversion tracks how credible and considered the page looks more than how much it contains; added complexity does not compensate for weak presentation.
when: Deciding where to spend limited effort on a product's marketing page.
fails: Presentation polish substituting for a clear value proposition — a beautiful page that never states what the product does still fails.

claim: Start a visual identity from one anchor image that already carries the mood you want, then derive palette, texture and type from it — rather than starting from a colour picker or a UI template.
why: An image encodes a coherent set of hues, contrasts and lighting that already read as a single mood; deriving from it guarantees the parts cohere, whereas assembling colours independently tends to produce an arbitrary or default look.
when: Kicking off brand or landing-page direction for a product whose differentiator is feel or atmosphere.
fails: Products needing strict brand-guideline compliance or heavy data/utility UI, where a fixed accessible token system must lead and imagery is decoration.

claim: Sample your base palette by eyedropping colours directly out of your chosen imagery instead of inventing hex values.
why: Colours lifted from a photograph are already harmonised by the light in that scene, so the UI sits with the imagery rather than fighting it.
when: Image-led marketing sites, hero-driven landing pages, any layout where photography occupies large surface area.
fails: Photo-derived colours are often low-contrast against each other; text and interactive states still need contrast-checked values, not raw samples.

claim: Reject both stock light mode and stock dark mode as starting points; commit to a specific tonal register (e.g. dark and warm, or bright and saturated) that expresses the brand.
why: Default light reads sterile and default flat dark reads generic — neither communicates anything specific about the product, so the site feels interchangeable with every other AI-built site.
when: Any site whose competitive problem is looking templated or indistinguishable.
fails: Accessibility-critical or long-session reading contexts where user-controlled light/dark and standard contrast are the priority.

claim: Prepare hero imagery with a consistent treatment chain — crop tight, darken, overlay fine noise/grain — before layering type on top.
why: Darkening buys text contrast without a scrim box, and grain removes the flat digital-gradient quality that makes dark UIs look default; applying the same chain to every image makes a mixed image set look like one collection.
when: Photographic heroes and section backgrounds carrying overlaid wordmarks or headlines.
fails: Product screenshots or detail shots where darkening and grain destroy the legibility of what's being shown.

claim: Supplement image-sampled base tones with two or three deliberate accent colours chosen from a curated palette source, and reserve them for feature icons and interactive elements.
why: Photo-derived earthy tones cluster in a narrow range and give nothing to highlight with; accents restore hierarchy and let icons carry meaning.
when: Dark, low-chroma palettes that need points of emphasis.
fails: Using more accents than the interface has meaning-levels, which flattens the hierarchy the accents were meant to create.

claim: Choose imagery whose subject matter names the product's domain — show the objects a user of the product actually handles.
why: Subject matter carries semantic information for free: the props tell the visitor what the product is for before they read a word, while also supplying texture to break up flat surfaces.
when: Products with a concrete real-world domain that photographs well.
fails: Abstract or infrastructure products with no photographable subject, where literal imagery becomes stock-photo filler.

claim: Audit the existing typeface stack part by part — keep what works, cut what doesn't — instead of replacing the whole system.
why: Type problems are usually localised to one member of the pairing; wholesale replacement discards a face that was already carrying the brand correctly.
when: Redesigning an existing site that has some functioning typographic choices.

claim: Drop monospace as a personality face on consumer-facing marketing pages; pair the workhorse sans with a serif when you want warmth and character.
why: Monospace reads as technical/default and adds no distinctiveness; a serif imports the associations of print — editorial, crafted, considered — which is a specific feeling rather than a neutral one.
when: Brand and marketing surfaces where the goal is personality, not code display.
fails: Interfaces where monospace is functional — code blocks, terminal output, aligned numeric columns.

claim: Pick your reference metaphor for the type treatment (e.g. a printed menu, a field guide, a technical manual) and let it decide the serif, the sizes and the spacing.
why: A concrete physical reference makes typographic decisions checkable — you can ask whether a choice moves toward or away from the reference — where abstract goals like 'more personality' cannot be evaluated.
when: Choosing between several technically-acceptable typeface pairings.
fails: The metaphor is unrelated to the product's actual use, producing a costume rather than an identity.

claim: Assemble the identity in dependency order — anchor image, then base palette, then accents, then texture, then type, then icons, then logo mark — so each layer is chosen against what already exists.
why: Later decisions have more constraints than earlier ones; choosing the logo mark before the palette means re-deciding it, while choosing icons after the accents exist means the accents dictate the icon colours.
when: Building a visual identity from nothing under time pressure.

claim: Judge every identity decision against 'does this convey the intended feeling for this specific brand' rather than against a checklist or a generation formula.
why: Formulaic systems produce internally-consistent but interchangeable results — exactly the failure mode of AI-generated sites — because they optimise for validity rather than for a particular feeling.
when: Any point in the identity process where a rule and the intended mood disagree.
fails: Used as licence to skip accessibility floors and legibility minimums, which are constraints rather than stylistic preferences.

claim: Design each section as a stack applied in fixed order: background fill or image, then texture, then type, then supporting UI, then layered imagery, then edge treatment.
why: Working in a fixed order turns visual design into a repeatable procedure, so later sections take a fraction of the decisions the first one did and stay consistent with each other.
when: Rendering a multi-section landing page from an approved wireframe.
fails: The order is treated as mandatory content — a section may legitimately skip texture or imagery; the sequence governs decision order, not required layers.

claim: Pull section backgrounds from the brand's defined colour set or image library rather than picking new colours at layout time.
why: Constraining backgrounds to already-decided identity assets is what keeps sections reading as one page instead of a series of unrelated screens.
when: A visual identity (palette, imagery, icon set) has been defined before layout begins.

claim: Overlay a subtle noise texture on flat or photographic backgrounds when text sits on top of them.
why: Noise adds surface interest to an otherwise dead fill and slightly breaks up the underlying value, which improves the separation between text and background.
when: Hero and media-backed sections carrying headline copy.
fails: The section is meant to read as clean, precise software — there, drop noise entirely and use a flat light fill.

claim: Match texture choice to the feeling the section needs: noise for warmth and grit, heavier noise over photography, graph-paper grids for technical or product sections, and no texture for clean software surfaces.
why: Texture is a tone signal, so varying it per section lets one page shift register without abandoning the shared system.
when: Sections in the same page serve different emotional jobs (emotional hero vs. rational feature explainer).

claim: Split a headline across two typefaces or styles rather than setting the whole thing in one sans-serif.
why: An all-sans headline is the safe default and reads generic; splitting the line gives the page a distinguishing detail at the highest-attention point.
when: Hero headlines where the page needs to feel unique, and where the split is anchored to something in the source brand or reference.
fails: The split is arbitrary — it should follow a meaningful break in the line, and doing it in every headline on the page cheapens the effect.

claim: Set the gap between subtext and the buttons below it to roughly twice the gap between headline and subtext.
why: Headline and subtext are one semantic unit and should sit close; the CTA is a separate unit and needs visible separation to read as a distinct step.
when: Stacked hero content of headline, supporting line, and one or more buttons.

claim: Measure vertical spacing from the text baseline, not the text bounding box, because a large heading carries built-in descender space below its baseline that already reads as gap.
why: Large type has proportionally large internal leading, so equal numerical margins look unequal — the heading's gap appears bigger than it was set.
when: Spacing anything directly beneath oversized display type.

claim: Make scattered imagery follow explicit rules: larger elements sit lower in the composition, smaller elements sit above them, and every element keeps a clear margin around the text block.
why: Randomness that is actually structured reads as energetic rather than messy, and the size-by-height gradient gives the scatter an implied depth and weight.
when: Hero or feature sections decorated with multiple floating image assets or product shots.
fails: Genuinely random placement — without the size gradient and text safety margin, the same assets read as clutter and hurt legibility.

claim: Reserve an untouched safety margin around every text block that no decorative asset may enter.
why: Copy is the section's payload; anything crowding it costs both legibility and the sense that the layout is deliberate.
when: Any composition layering decoration over or beside type.

claim: Darken the outer edges of a busy section with a vignette to steer the eye to the centre content.
why: Reducing brightness at the frame edges lowers the visual pull of peripheral decoration so the headline and CTA win attention.
when: Sections with imagery or texture running to the edges that compete with centred copy.
fails: Clean, light, flat-background sections where a vignette would read as a heavy-handed artifact.

claim: Scale typography down per section as you move past the hero — hero display size, then mid-size for following narrative sections.
why: A descending type scale across sections encodes the page hierarchy and stops every section from shouting equally.
when: Long-scroll landing pages with several full-width sections.

claim: Let imagery dominate the page in feature sections, paired with icons drawn from the brand deck rather than a generic icon set.
why: Large product imagery does the explaining, and brand-derived icons keep the supporting detail inside the identity instead of importing a foreign visual voice.
when: Sections demonstrating product capability.

claim: Finish the layout and the visual identity as separate artifacts so a different identity can be dropped into the same layout.
why: Decoupling them means one structural investment yields many distinct-feeling pages, and it lets you test emotional direction without re-solving hierarchy.
when: Any landing page where direction may change, or where multiple brands or variants share a page structure.
fails: The layout was implicitly designed around one identity's asset shapes or colour count — then the swap breaks and the layout needs rework.

claim: Before deleting decorative elements in the name of minimalism, check what each one communicates; keep any element that lets a first-time visitor infer the product category without reading copy.
why: Illustrations and objects carry semantic payload, not just visual weight — stripping them can leave a layout that is technically cleaner but emptier and less informative.
when: Editing a busy hero or landing page, or resisting the default instinct to simplify.
fails: The elements are generic ornament with no relationship to the product — then removal genuinely does clarify.

claim: Build a decorated hero as a centred text core with supporting objects arranged around it, never on top of or crowding it.
why: The composition reads as a subject with context when the message holds the centre; decoration that migrates inward becomes competition for the same attention.
when: Landing page or hero sections that need personality beyond a headline and button.

claim: Preserve a generous clear zone around headline and body copy; the size of that untouched margin is what distinguishes contextual decoration from clutter.
why: The presenter identifies spacing around text as the single shared property across all the reference designs that succeed.
when: Any layout where illustrations, badges, or ornaments sit near type.

claim: Do not fill every remaining pocket of whitespace with decoration — leaving an asymmetric empty region is correct, and adding one more element to 'balance' it usually tips the design into clutter.
why: Demonstrated directly: an extra illustration dropped into leftover space visibly crosses the threshold.
when: Late-stage decoration passes where the temptation is to even out the composition.

claim: Angle, position, and scale decorative elements so they point or lean toward the centre of the composition rather than away from it.
why: Off-grid elements act as directional cues; when they aim outward they leak attention away from the message even though no explicit rule is violated.
when: Free-floating, non-grid-aligned decoration around a centred hero.

claim: Reduce the density, size, or opacity of decorative elements as they move away from the focal point, so the edges of the canvas trail off rather than terminate abruptly.
why: A gradient of visual weight from centre outward reinforces the hierarchy and keeps the frame from feeling walled in.
when: Scattered-object hero compositions.

claim: When elements are placed off-grid, accept that alignment becomes an eyeballed judgement call and budget iteration time for it — do not expect grid rules or auto-layout to resolve placement for you.
why: The grid is the usual arbiter of position; abandoning it transfers that responsibility to the designer's eye.
when: Deliberately breaking the box for expressive layouts.
fails: Dense, content-heavy, or systematised interfaces where grid discipline is doing real work.

claim: Pick an illustration style that matches the product's position on a playful-to-professional axis: blobs, bright colour, and characters for playful products; realistic, rendered imagery for serious ones.
why: The decoration sets tone as much as it sets context, so a mismatch between imagery style and product seriousness undermines credibility.
when: Choosing between illustration systems — 3D renders, doodles, neo-brutalist shapes, photography.

claim: Locate two or three reference sites that bracket your intended tone and place your design explicitly between them before committing to a style.
why: Positioning against concrete anchors turns a vague aesthetic goal into a decision you can check your work against.
when: Starting a visual direction for a landing page.

claim: Search reference libraries by tone attribute rather than by industry, so you can study how other teams solved the same expressive problem regardless of product category.
why: The transferable knowledge is in the treatment, not the vertical.
when: Gathering visual research at the start of a project.

claim: When you need a gradient that sits next to a photograph, eyedrop the colours out of that photograph instead of choosing them from a colour picker.
why: Sampled colours inherit the photo's exact hue, saturation and lighting cast, so the gradient reads as an extension of the image rather than a separate graphic element pasted beside it.
when: A flat colour field, gradient, or background sits directly adjacent to or beneath photographic content.
fails: The photo's dominant colours conflict with brand or accessibility requirements for the text sitting on that gradient — then the sample is a starting point, not the final value.

claim: To extend a colour region in a photo, duplicate the image, flip it vertically, and crop the mirrored copy down to the strip you need, rather than reaching for generative fill.
why: The mirrored copy is made of the same pixels, so grain, gradient falloff and colour cast match perfectly and the seam disappears — no model output to inspect for artefacts or hallucinated detail.
when: A photo needs more of one colour or texture at an edge, and that edge region is soft, blurred, or low-detail (sky, wall, gradient falloff).
fails: The edge contains recognisable structure — faces, text, hard geometry, a horizon line — where a mirrored copy produces an obvious duplicate or impossible symmetry.

claim: Zoom to inspect a colour field before assuming it is flat; a region that looks like solid brand colour at page scale is often a gradient that dilutes toward the crop edge.
why: Perceived colour at thumbnail size averages the region, hiding the falloff that becomes obvious once the image is placed full-bleed on a large viewport.
when: Judging whether a photo carries enough of a brand colour to anchor a section.

claim: When product variants are visually near-identical, do not rely on the product photo to communicate the difference; assign each variant a distinct colour treatment on its card and let text carry the specifics.
why: The photo cannot do differentiating work it does not contain, so the card container has to take over the signalling role.
when: Building comparison layouts for trims, tiers, sizes, or SKUs whose photography does not visually distinguish them.
fails: The colour assignment is arbitrary and unrelated to the actual variant — users then read the colour as the product's colour rather than as a category marker.

claim: If the only available imagery is mediocre and cannot be replaced, crop or occlude it so only a usable sliver shows, and let the following section overlap the rest.
why: Image quality only has to hold up over the area you actually reveal; hiding the weak portion buys texture and colour presence without exposing the flaws.
when: An image is decorative or supporting rather than informational, and better source material is genuinely unavailable.
fails: The image is load-bearing — the user needs to see the product to make the decision — in which case cropping it away removes the information the section exists to deliver.

claim: Before spending effort improving an asset, ask whether the section actually depends on it; if not, downgrade the asset's prominence instead of upgrading its quality.
why: Effort should track how much the element carries the section's job; non-essential elements can be reduced rather than perfected.
when: Blocked on sourcing or producing a high-quality asset for a supporting element.

claim: When one section's copy runs far longer than the rest of the page, collapse the surplus behind a 'see more' control instead of letting that section break the page's text rhythm.
why: A page establishes an expected density of text per section; one section that violates it reads as heavy and stalls scanning, even when the content itself is worth keeping.
when: Necessary detail (specs, disclosures, long descriptions) exceeds the text budget the rest of the layout has set.
fails: The long copy is the primary reason the user is on that section — hiding decision-critical detail behind an extra click costs more than the visual consistency gains.

claim: Reveal expanded content by sliding a panel up over the card's image on hover, keeping the card's outer footprint fixed.
why: Animating within the existing bounds avoids reflowing neighbouring columns, and the image area is the part of the card most expendable once the user has committed attention to that variant.
when: Card grids on pointer devices where each card has a large image region and secondary detail text.
fails: Touch input, where there is no hover state — the reveal needs a tap target and an explicit close, or the content stays hidden permanently.

claim: Judge each section against the page's established text-to-visual ratio, not against itself in isolation.
why: Consistency of density is what makes a page feel like one system; a section that is fine standalone can still be wrong in sequence.
when: Reviewing a long-scroll page section by section.

claim: Use a sticker/badge when a layout has gone visually rigid — place it so it overlaps or breaks the edge of a card, section, or grid cell, giving the composition one deliberate escape from its boxes.
why: A layout built entirely from aligned rectangles reads as flat and monotonous; a rotated, irregular shape crossing a boundary creates a focal contrast and implies depth.
when: Marketing pages, pricing sections, hero areas, or product cards where the underlying grid is doing all the visual work and nothing draws the eye.
fails: Dense functional UI (dashboards, tables, forms) where an off-grid decorative element competes with data, and in any layout where stickers appear often enough to become the new baseline rather than the exception.

claim: Build the sticker shape from a polygon/star primitive with a high point count (around 12), then tune the inner-radius ratio and apply corner rounding rather than drawing the outline by hand.
why: A parametric primitive keeps points evenly distributed and stays editable, so the spikiness and softness can be dialled in as two independent sliders instead of redrawn.
when: Creating burst, seal, flower, or scallop-style sticker silhouettes in a vector tool.
fails: Asymmetric or hand-drawn sticker styles, where the mechanical regularity of a generated star is the wrong character.

claim: Set sticker labels in a quirky display typeface, deliberately different from the product's UI and body typefaces.
why: The sticker is meant to read as a pasted-on object from outside the interface; borrowing the system font makes it read as just another UI chip and cancels the effect.
when: Short sticker copy — a few words at most, at large size.
fails: Long or information-critical copy, or brands with a strict single-typeface mandate; display faces lose legibility at small sizes and in long strings.

claim: Give depth with a hard drop shadow: zero or near-zero blur, 100% opacity, offset a few pixels, coloured as a darker shade of the sticker's own fill rather than transparent black.
why: A blurred grey shadow reads as generic elevation; a solid same-hue offset reads as a printed die-cut object and keeps the sticker chromatically unified instead of muddying the fill.
when: Flat, illustrative, or sticker-style graphics where a tangible printed feel is the goal.
fails: Systems using a soft, physically-modelled elevation scale — mixing a hard offset shadow into that vocabulary breaks the material logic.

claim: Layer secondary detail onto the sticker — an offset stroke that traces the silhouette, and a short line of text bent along a circular path with a text-on-path plugin — but only one or two such treatments per sticker.
why: A single flat shape with one word reads as unfinished; a second concentric detail supplies the visual density that makes it feel like a designed seal, while stacking every treatment at once turns it into noise.
when: Larger stickers with enough surface area for a ring of text or a visible outline offset.
fails: Small stickers, where curved microtype becomes unreadable and the outline collapses into the fill.

claim: Treat stickers as the designated place in the system to be maximalist: vary the silhouette, saturation, and internal pattern between instances instead of tokenising them into one repeated component.
why: Their job is disruption, so consistency across instances defeats the purpose — while the surrounding UI still holds the system discipline.
when: Expressive brand surfaces where exactly one or two elements are allowed to break the system.
fails: Where stickers carry functional meaning (status, discount tier) and users must be able to compare them — then they need consistent, decodable treatment.

claim: Reserve high-chroma decorative fills like a kaleidoscope/radial-gradient pattern for dark backgrounds.
why: Saturated multi-hue patterns need a dark field to hold their contrast; on light backgrounds the light bands of the pattern wash out and the shape loses its edge.
when: Dark-theme surfaces where a sticker or button is meant to glow as the brightest element on screen.
fails: Light themes, or anywhere text sits on top of the pattern and contrast cannot be guaranteed across its bands.

claim: Treat image selection and presentation as a primary design decision, not decorative filler.
why: Images occupy substantial visual space, so weak imagery can undermine an otherwise solid layout.
when: Designing pages where photos, products, or hero visuals are prominent.

claim: Use AI-generated images only when they suit the project’s context and visual needs.
why: High image quality alone does not guarantee that generated visuals fit the brand, subject, or available assets.
when: You need new visual assets and have flexibility in image sourcing.
fails: Authentic, supplied, regulated, or context-specific photography is required.

claim: For a photo with one clear subject, remove its background and let the subject extend beyond its container.
why: An isolated subject receives more attention and can break the uniform boxed-card feel.
when: The image has a distinct foreground object or person that can be cleanly separated.
fails: The subject boundary is ambiguous or the surrounding context is essential to the image’s meaning.

claim: For product visuals, crop tightly and enlarge a compelling detail instead of always showing the entire product.
why: A close crop makes the product feel more dramatic and visually engaging.
when: A product has recognizable details, texture, or form that remain legible when cropped.
fails: Users need a full-object view to understand the product or compare key features.

claim: For landscape or wide-angle imagery, place a readable overlay over the image and use it as a brand-message panel.
why: The image creates atmosphere while the text delivers a high-impact message in the same section.
when: You have wide imagery with sufficient quiet space or can create contrast beneath text.
fails: The overlay makes copy illegible or obscures the visual detail the image needs to communicate.

claim: Mask images into shapes that repeat the website’s visual language.
why: Custom image silhouettes make the composition feel more intentional and distinctive than standard rectangles.
when: The brand already has a clear shape language that can be echoed in imagery.
fails: The mask harms recognition, clips important content, or adds visual novelty without serving the design system.
